newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's PDVSA launches small investor bonds.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's PDVSA launches small investor bonds.

text.p: Venezuela's state owned oil company PDVSA on Friday launched its first small investor bonds intended to encourage local participation in Venezuela's booming oil industry.

Eduardo Lima, director of PDVSA subsidiary SOFIP, said the first issue was a 30 billion bolivar ($63 million) three-year par bond with a coupon set between the domestic 90-day commercial deposit rate and A-rated domestic commercial paper. The rate would be adjusted every three months and the issue date was set for February 27 1997.
The bond will be released in three tranches over three weeks, with priority given to individuals investing between 100,000 and 1,000,000 bolivars ($210-$2100).
Lima said the bond represented the first part of a planned 60 billion bolivar ($130 million) debt programme for small investors over three years, all guaranteed by PDVSA.

Later this year, SOFIP also planned to launch a scheme to allow small shareholders and international investors up to a 10 percent share in Venezuela's 20 marginal oil fields under the government's third oil licensing round.

Private capital, mostly belonging to big multinational oil companies, is already flooding into Venezuelan oil exploration and production through various profit-sharing contracts, operating agreements and joint ventures.
"In the same way, the opening (of the oil industry) also involves the participation of Venezuelan citizens," Lima said.
He hoped the bond would encourage Venezuela's domestic capital markets and contribute to PDVSA's $65 billion investment plan over the next ten years.
Under the forthcoming share scheme, investors would bear their share of the project costs in exchange for a slice of the revenues that PDVSA pays to the private consortium.
Lima said SOFIP was also studying other potential investment opportunities, including low risk exploration, strategic associations in the Orinoco Tar Belt and various service contracts.
In the long term, he hoped to extend investment opportunities to downstream activities like refining and petrochemicals.
